# What is albedo?

Albedo can be thought of as a surface reflectance value given from 0 to 1, where 0 is a perfect blackbody, and 1 is a perfect reflector. Albedo value can tell us about the composition of the surface (i.e. broadleaf has higher values than conifer, snow has very high values while burnt areas are closer to 0). Albedo also plays an important role in the surface-energy budget, by indicating how much incoming radiation is absorbed or reflected. Values near 0 represent greater absorption, while values near 1 represent greater reflectance. Higher albedos can contribute to net regional cooling, while lower albedos can contribute to net regional warming.


# albedofindr

<!-- badges: start -->
<!-- badges: end -->

The goal of albedofindr is to calculate albedo for Landsat versions 5, 7, and 8, using Liang et al's (2001) narrowband-to-broadband conversion linear regression. Landsat does not have a native albedo product, so it is calculated as follows for Landsat 5, 7, and 8:

$$
\frac{0.356 \cdot Blue + 0.130 \cdot Red + 0.373 \cdot NIR + 0.085 \cdot SWIR1 + 0.072 \cdot SWIR2 - 0.0018}{1.016}
$$


**IMPORTANT CAVEAT** : Liang et al (2001) tends to overestimate albedo (when compared to MODIS), especially in the winter. It is highly recommended to only use this package for summer albedo calculations. While the calculation within the package is clamped to [0,1], the equation itself is unbounded, and is therefore, unreliable. The equation was also derived only using summer imagery.

## Important Notes 

1. **IMPORTANT CAVEAT** : Liang et al (2001) tends to overestimate albedo (when compared to MODIS), especially in the winter. It is highly recommended to only use this package for summer albedo calculations, as the equation was derived only using summer imagery. While the calculation within the package is clamped to [0,1], the equation itself is unbounded, and is therefore, is capable of producing unrealistic results. 
1. This package requires the use of a **Python Environment**. I followed [this tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olNYYynSJfI) to get set up.
1. This package is dependent on **Google Earth Engine** (example given in Vignettes section), please use
your Google Earth Engine credentials. 

## Installation

You can install the development version of albedofindr from [GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("hesses167/albedofindr")
```

## Output

This package can be used to calculate albedo, compile an albedo collection with a date 
range and region as set by the user, and lastly, produce a median albedo composite TIF, 
also within a specified date range and region. The output can be used for analysis, or 
to visually display differences in albedo across a region of interest. Such an example 
is given here:

```{r example-albedo, echo = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("data-raw/final_vignette"))
```
